archetype.name: Pretender (power-play propped)
archetype.definition: Edmonton's record runs well ahead of its 5-on-5 play: a top-two power play and above-average even-strength percentages are covering for a team that is being out-chanced most nights.

report.headline: First in the Pacific on special teams and percentages, not on territory
report.take:
On the standings page Edmonton looks like a juggernaut. It is 17-5-4 and leads the Pacific, sits fifth in Goal Diff / GP at 0.92, scores 3.88 goals a game (third), and is on pace for 120 points and 54 wins. The site is less impressed and ranks the Oilers seventh. That gap is the story of the season. Behind the scoreboard, Edmonton is a below-average 5-on-5 team.

The engine is the power play. At 32.6% it ranks second, ten points above the league's 22.5%. That is no fluke for this franchise: it ran at 32.4% in 2022-23 and 30.6% last season, so a good share of it should hold. The other prop is even-strength percentages. The 5-on-5 PDO sits at 103.3, and Pts vs Goal Diff adds another 2.2 points from close games. Goaltending has helped quietly too. Tristan Jarry (.907, 1.8 GSAx, two shutouts) and Devon Levi (.896) have the team at +0.9 GSAx and an A- grade. After four straight seasons of negative GSAx, bottoming at -12.2 in 2022-23, merely average-plus goaltending is a real change.

What the record hides is territory. Edmonton's xGF % is 46.5% and its CF % is 47%, both 25th in the league. For years this was a team that drove play: 58.2% xGF in 2023-24 and 54.5% the season after. It slipped to 51.7% last year and has now fallen below water. The penalty kill (77.6%, 17th) is ordinary, and the Forwards grade is a D. The defense also lets wingers take 57.1% of the points it allows, against a league share of 43%. In other words, the Oilers are winning the special-teams and shooting-luck columns and losing the 5-on-5 shot battle. That mix tends to look worse as the sample grows.

The early signs are already showing. October was 10-3 with 4.23 goals a game. November came in at 7-5 and 3.42. The last five games went 2-2-1, with 19 goals scored and 19 allowed, and a road trip that closed with losses at Tampa Bay, Carolina and St. Louis. None of this threatens a playoff spot in a Pacific where only Vegas is keeping pace. But a 120-point team this is not, and the gap between its record and its play is what decides whether it is a real contender come spring.

strengths.title: An elite, repeatable power play
strengths.body: At 32.6% the power play ranks second and sits ten points above the league average. It is the single biggest reason Edmonton scores at the third-best rate. History says it is mostly real: it ran 32.4% in 2022-23 and 30.6% last year, so expect some cooling but not a collapse.

strengths.title: Goaltending finally pulling its weight
strengths.body: The tandem has a positive team GSAx of 0.9 and an A- grade, after last season's -7.7. Jarry carries most of the value at 1.8 GSAx, while Levi has been roughly average at 0.0. That is sustainable as long as Jarry keeps getting his share of the starts. It is a floor-raiser rather than a game-stealer.

strengths.title: Scoring volume across the board
strengths.body: Edmonton scores 3.88 goals a game, 0.68 above the league rate. It also keeps goals against to 2.96, eighth-best, so the 0.92 Goal Diff / GP is not built on one end of the ice. Even through November's slowdown it put up 3.42 a game, which is still a strong number.

concerns.title: Losing the 5-on-5 territory battle
concerns.body: Edmonton ranks 25th in both xGF % (46.5%) and CF % (47%), so it spends more time defending than attacking at even strength. This is a sharp break from a franchise that was at 58.2% xGF two seasons ago. It is the clearest sign that the record overstates the team, and it is the hardest thing on this list to fix mid-season.

concerns.title: Percentages and close games inflating the record
concerns.body: A 5-on-5 PDO of 103.3 is well above the 100 baseline. Pts vs Goal Diff adds 2.2 standings points, seventh-most in the league. Both usually drift back toward average. When they do, a team that is out-chanced at even strength will give some of those wins back.

concerns.title: Goals against creeping up lately
concerns.body: Over the last five games Edmonton allowed 3.8 a game, 0.84 worse than its season rate. It gave up seven in Carolina and five in both the Anaheim and St. Louis losses. With an ordinary penalty kill (77.6%, 17th) and a defense that leaks points to wingers, the slide fits the underlying numbers more than it looks like a blip.

trend.note: A 10-3 October with 4.23 goals a game gave way to a 7-5 November at 3.42. The last five games went 2-2-1 with an even goal differential, as the gap between Edmonton's results and its 5-on-5 play started to close.

weekAhead.headline: Division showdown with Vegas, then two soft games with Seattle
weekAhead.body:
The week opens at home against Vegas (14-6-5, site rank 5), the only Pacific team close enough to threaten Edmonton's lead. It is also the kind of opponent that exposes the Oilers' weakness. Vegas owns a 53.3% xGF share, eighth in the league, against Edmonton's 46.5%. The Knights also bring an A-graded blueline and a power play ranked fourth. Expect Vegas to tilt the ice, which leaves Edmonton needing its power play and Jarry-or-Levi goaltending to win it.

Then comes a home-and-home with Seattle (10-9-1, site rank 30), which is about as good a draw as the schedule offers. The Kraken are last in CF % at 42%, 28th in xGF %, 28th in goals against, and their penalty kill is last in the league at 60.7%. Their defense gives up points to wingers well beyond expectation, ranking 30th. Against the league's second-best power play, Seattle's penalty trouble is a mismatch. Taking at least three of four points there is the reasonable expectation, even with the Kraken's 102.6 PDO propping them up.

keyMatchups.title: Oilers power play vs Kraken penalty kill
keyMatchups.body: Edmonton converts 32.6% of its chances, second in the league. Seattle kills only 60.7%, last in the league. Every Seattle penalty is close to a coin-flip goal against this unit, so discipline will decide how lopsided those two games get.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas puck possession at 5-on-5
keyMatchups.body: Vegas sits at 53.3% xGF and 51% CF, both eighth, while Edmonton is 25th in both. The Knights' defense has held centers to a tiny 5% share of the points against it. Edmonton will likely be chasing play and will need its special teams to carry the night.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's leaky defense against wingers
keyMatchups.body: Seattle allows 0.95 points a game to wingers, 0.33 above expectation and 30th in the league, and 29.9 shots against a game. After a road trip where Edmonton's own defense sagged, this is a chance for its forwards to rebuild some margin.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Edmonton can play Vegas close at 5-on-5, or again has to lean on the power play and goaltending to beat a team that out-chances it.

restOfSeason.body:
The 120-point pace will not hold. The 103.3 PDO and the 2.2 points of close-game luck should fade. Without them, a team in the bottom third in xGF % and CF % plays closer to its November form than its October form. What should last is the power play, which has a multi-year track record, plus better goaltending than Edmonton has had in recent seasons. That is enough to keep it comfortably in the playoff picture, especially in a Pacific where most of the division is at or below .500. A finish in the range of 98 to 110 points and 45 to 51 wins is the realistic band, with the goal margin shrinking toward something like 0.4 to 0.7 a game.

The bigger question is spring. Unless Edmonton's even-strength play recovers toward the 51.7% xGF of last season, it is a team that wins the regular season on special teams and percentages. Playoff opponents are less likely to hand it that many power plays. The division title is in reach with Vegas as the main rival. The contender label has to be earned at 5-on-5.

confidence.note: 26 games is a real sample and the possession numbers are consistent, but the roster detail in the sheet is thin.
